section.title: Judgment on Judah's Leaders
section.sectionRationale: This movement continues the opening arraignment by turning from the nation as a whole to its collapsing leadership: every prop of stable society, warrior, judge, elder, counselor, is removed, leaving anarchy, oppression of the poor by corrupt rulers, and the haughty daughters of Zion stripped of their finery. The seam ends with a desperate image of seven women grasping one man, society's structures utterly unraveled.
section.thesis: When a people forsakes the LORD, He withdraws the very supports that hold society together, exposing the oppression of the poor by their own leaders and stripping away the pride, both of rulers and of the fashionable elite, that masked the rot beneath.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the LORD removes every prop and support from Jerusalem and Judah; society collapses into oppression and reversal; the LORD's indictment of the elders and the haughty daughters of Zion; and the resulting desolation, ending with women pleading just to bear a man's name.

units.label: Every support removed
units.note: warrior, judge, elder, and counselor taken away

verses.text: For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support: the whole supply of food and water,
the mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the soothsayer and the elder,
the commander of fifty and the dignitary, the counselor, the cunning magician, and the clever enchanter.
“I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.”
The people will oppress one another, man against man, neighbor against neighbor; the young will rise up against the old, and the base against the honorable.
A man will seize his brother within his father's house: “You have a cloak, you be our leader! Take charge of this heap of rubble.”
On that day he will cry aloud: “I am not a healer. I have no food or clothing in my house. Do not make me leader of the people!”
For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD, defying His glorious presence.

The expression on their faces testifies against them, and like Sodom they flaunt their sin; 
they do not conceal it. Woe to them, for they have brought disaster upon themselves.
Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor.
Woe to the wicked; disaster is upon them! For they will be repaid with what their hands have done.
Youths oppress My people, and women rule over them. O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths.

units.label: The LORD's charge against the leaders

verses.text: The LORD arises to {{riv|contend}}; He stands to judge the people.
The LORD brings this charge against the elders and leaders of His people: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses.
Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.

The LORD also says: 
“Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, walking with heads held high 
and wanton eyes, prancing and skipping as they go, jingling the bracelets on their ankles,

the Lord will bring sores on the heads of the daughters of Zion, 
and the LORD will make their foreheads bare. ”
In that day the Lord will take away their finery: their anklets and headbands and crescents;
their pendants, bracelets, and veils;
their headdresses, ankle chains, and sashes; their perfume bottles and charms;
their signet rings and nose rings;
their festive robes, capes, cloaks, and purses;
and their mirrors, linen garments, tiaras, and shawls.
Instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, sackcloth; instead of beauty, shame.
Your men will fall by the sword, and your warriors in battle.
And the gates of Zion will lament and mourn; destitute, she will sit on the ground.
In that day seven women will take hold of one man and say, “We will eat our own bread and provide our own clothes. Just let us be called by your name. Take away our disgrace!”

riv.gloss: A legal dispute, contention, or lawsuit. The LORD rises to riv, to bring formal charges against His own leaders, continuing the covenant lawsuit begun in chapter 1, now directed specifically at those responsible for justice who instead crushed the poor.

basic.context: This chapter zooms in from the nation as a whole to its leadership. God announces He will strip away every stabilizing figure, warriors, judges, elders, counselors, leaving society in chaos where the young oppress the old and no one wants the burden of leading a ruined people. At the center, God specifically charges the elders and rulers with crushing the poor, and the proud, fashionable daughters of Zion with vanity while the nation crumbles.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, specific coming judgment on Judah's actual social and political structures, likely realized in the chaos and depopulation following Assyrian incursions or the eventual Babylonian conquest, not a timeless allegory about any society. The uncomfortable emphasis is that God's judgment falls with particular force on leaders and the privileged; those who had the most responsibility for justice bear the sharpest indictment for its absence.
basic.originalLanguages: The LORD rises to riv, to bring a formal legal charge, against His own elders and princes, the very people entrusted with justice. The specific accusation is vivid: they have devoured the vineyard and ground the faces of the poor, images of violent, personal exploitation rather than abstract mismanagement.
basic.typology: The collapse of righteous leadership here, until no one is willing to lead a ruined people, sets up the need for the true and willing Shepherd-King promised later in Isaiah, who will not shirk the burden of His people but will lay down His life for them.
basic.christ: Where these leaders devoured the vineyard entrusted to them and crushed the poor they were meant to protect, Christ is the true Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and the true King who defends the cause of the poor and needy, Psalm 72:4, Luke 4:18. His willing leadership answers the desperate cry of verse 3:7, do not make me leader of the people, a burden every human ruler eventually refuses or fails to bear rightly.
basic.god: God holds leaders to greater accountability than those they lead, since He entrusted them with justice for the vulnerable. His judgment is not random collapse but the deliberate, controlled removal of the very supports a rebellious society had trusted instead of Him, exposing that their stability was never really in warriors, counselors, or fine clothing.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34:2-4 likewise condemns shepherds who feed themselves rather than the flock. James 5:1-6 echoes this indictment of the wealthy who have defrauded the poor. John 10:11-14 contrasts hired hands who flee with the good shepherd who lays down His life. Micah 3:1-3, addressed to the same era's leaders, uses nearly identical imagery of devouring the people like flesh.
basic.oneStory: This chapter shows what happens when a society's leaders fail the trust God gave them: the whole structure collapses, and no human leader is finally willing or able to bear the weight. That failure sets the stage for the true King later promised in Isaiah, who bears His people's burden all the way to the cross.

context.literary:
The passage is a descent in three steps, and each step is marked by the phrase 'in that day' or by a change of speaker. Verses 1 to 7 are an announcement in the third person that the Lord GOD of Hosts will remove every support, and they unfold as a list that starts with food and water, moves through the warrior, judge, prophet and elder, and ends with the enchanter. The list is a sweep from the physical to the political to the religious, and the last two entries show that even the false sources of guidance will go. Verses 8 to 15 turn to cause and courtroom: the cause is that Jerusalem has stumbled because her words and deeds were against the LORD, verse 8, and the court scene begins when the LORD 'arises to contend,' verse 13. Verses 16 to 4:1 are a second oracle, now addressed to the women of Zion, with a catalogue of finery that runs for six verses and a set of reversals that turns each item into its opposite.

The construction of verse 24 is the neatest piece of design. Five times the sentence says 'instead of' and sets a pleasant thing against a bitter one, perfume against a stench, a belt against a rope, styled hair against baldness, fine clothing against sackcloth, and beauty against shame. The reader has just walked through the adornments, item by item, and is now given the same march in reverse.

The unit also carries a short wisdom insert in verses 10 and 11 that says the righteous will eat the fruit of their works and the wicked will be repaid with what their hands have done. The principle is placed in the middle of the indictment as if to remind the audience that the verdict is not arbitrary. Chapter 4:1 closes the section with a bitter after-image of the war, and the next verse, 4:2, then breaks into hope.
context.historical:
Isaiah's audience was not poor. The eighth century BC in Judah was a time of consolidation under Uzziah and Jotham, with building projects, trade and armies, 2 Chronicles 26:9 to 15, and the inequality that follows prosperity. Isaiah 5:8 describes landowners who added house to house and field to field until no room was left for others, and Isaiah 10:1 and 2 names the officials who enact unjust statutes and deprive the poor of fair treatment. Chapter 3's verses 14 and 15 belong with them. Elders and leaders were the village and city rulers who sat in the gate and decided cases, and those were the people most able to take what belonged to the poor.

The list in verses 2 and 3 describes the organs of a functioning society in the ancient world: the soldier who defends, the judge who decides, the prophet and elder who counsel, and the craftsman and skilled speaker who keep the machinery running. It is also notable that the soothsayer, the magician and the enchanter appear on the same list. Isaiah does not consider them to be reliable guides, and he groups them with the leaders because the people consulted them. The removal of all of these comes in the crisis of war and exile, when the best were killed or deported. Second Kings 24:14 describes Nebuchadnezzar carrying off all the officers and fighting men and all the craftsmen and artisans, leaving only the poorest.

The women of verses 16 to 23 were the wives and daughters of that ruling class. The finery is a real inventory of ancient jewellery and dress, from ankle bracelets to signet rings to mirrors, and much of it was costly. Their strutting and jingling is the visible counterpart of the elders' greed. Verse 24's sackcloth, baldness and the sitting on the ground in verse 26 are the standard signs of mourning, found in Lamentations 2:10, and the war that kills the men in verse 25 produces the scene of 4:1, in which seven women plead with one man to give them his name.
context.canonical:
Prophets after Isaiah take up the charge against leaders almost word for word. Micah 3:1 to 3 asks whether the rulers of Israel should not know justice, and then describes them as those who hate good and strip the flesh of the people. Jeremiah 23:1 and 2 pronounces woe on the shepherds who scatter the flock. Ezekiel 34 is the longest development: the shepherds fed themselves, did not strengthen the weak or bind up the injured, and ruled with violence, so the LORD Himself will search for His sheep, Ezekiel 34:4 and 11 to 16. Zechariah 11:16 speaks of a shepherd who will not heal the broken but will devour the flesh of the choice sheep.

The judgment on the women of Zion has a counterpart in Amos 4:1, which condemns the women of Samaria who oppress the poor, and in Isaiah 32:9 to 14, where complacent women are told to tremble. The reverse of the desolate Zion that sits on the ground is found in Isaiah 47:1, where Babylon is told to sit in the dust, and in Lamentations 2:10, where the elders of the Daughter of Zion do the same. The cry for a name in Isaiah 4:1 is answered later when God Himself promises the barren and widowed city that her husband is her Maker, Isaiah 54:1 to 5.

The New Testament picks up the same ideas. James 5:1 to 6 addresses the rich who fattened themselves on withheld wages, and the principle of Isaiah 3:10 and 11 is restated in Galatians 6:7: God is not mocked, and whatever a man sows he will reap. Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Matthew 9:36, and Peter charges elders to shepherd the flock not for greed but willingly, not lording it over those in their charge, 1 Peter 5:2 and 3. Peter also says that the beauty of women should not come from outward adornment but from a gentle and quiet spirit, 1 Peter 3:3 and 4, which is a calm echo of the sharper words in Isaiah 3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah wanted the leaders and the privileged to hear that their security was already gone. The list of what the LORD will remove makes the point that the things they relied on, soldiers, judges, counsellors, even food and water, were never their own. They were supplied and supported, and the one who supplied them can take them away. The picture of a society so emptied that a man with a cloak is dragged forward to lead is meant to be absurd, and the absurdity is the point: a leaderless city will beg for anybody.

He also wanted them to see that the issue was not only the fall of the kingdom but the cause of it. Verse 8 names the cause in the plainest terms: their words and deeds were against the LORD. The detailed charges of verses 14 and 15 about the vineyard and the grinding of the poor give the cause a face. When the prophet then turns to the women, he does not mock them for liking beauty; he exposes that their finery was part of the same self-exalting posture that chapter 2 condemned in the men, and he prepares the way for the better beauty that will come in 4:2.

Finally, he meant to leave the hearer with a verse like 3:10, 'Tell the righteous it will be well with them.' Even inside a judgment oracle there is a protected category. The disaster has a moral shape, and the faithful will not be treated as the unfaithful.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes a coming judgment on a specific people. It does not give a rule for how societies should be run, and its image of children and women ruling is not a statement about the proper roles of the young or of women. In the prophet's world the reversal shows disorder: the weak and unprepared are pushed into positions that only experienced rulers can hold. Elsewhere in Scripture women such as Deborah lead with the LORD's approval, Judges 4:4 to 5:31, and Josiah became king as a boy to the nation's benefit, 2 Kings 22:1. The point here is the collapse of the structure, not who fills the role.\n\nThe list of finery is also descriptive. It is not a fashion code for believers. The apostles give their own, different guidance about adornment, 1 Timothy 2:9 and 1 Peter 3:3 and 4, and they keep the concern with the heart and the good works that flow from it. What does carry forward is the standard for those in authority: God holds elders, rulers and teachers responsible for how the weak are treated, James 3:1 and Hebrews 13:17. And the principle of 3:10 and 11 continues to give comfort and warning, since what people do returns on them in the long run.

debates.question: What is the point of the catalogue of finery in verses 18 to 23?

views.label: Vanity and misplaced trust
views.case: The long list pictures a society so absorbed in its appearance that it cannot see the collapse around it. The list of ornaments sits beside the list of idols, silver and horses in Isaiah 2:7 and 8, and both are things in which the people place their confidence.

views.label: The fruit of exploitation
views.case: Verses 14 and 15 charge the leaders with taking the plunder of the poor into their houses. The women's jewellery may therefore be the visible form of that plunder, and the judgment is on the wealth taken as much as on the women who wear it.

views.label: The women as leaders in a corrupt system
views.case: Amos 4:1 shows women of the ruling classes as active in the oppression of the poor. Isaiah may be addressing women who share in the culture of consumption that depends on the extraction from the poor, and who encourage it.

debates.bearing: All three readings locate the sin in what the finery stands for, not in the jewellery itself. The removal of the ornaments is the stripping of everything that made them feel secure, and the reversals of verse 24 match each luxury with its loss.

debates.question: Who rules in verse 12, 'women' or 'creditors'?

views.label: Women rule over the people
views.case: The traditional Hebrew text has the word for women, and the line then matches verses 4 and 5, where children rule and the young rise against the old. It reads as another sign of disordered leadership.

views.label: Creditors or exactors rule over the people
views.case: The same consonants can be read with different vowels to give 'creditors,' and some ancient translations and many modern scholars prefer this because it matches the immediate charge of crushing the poor in verses 14 and 15. The ruler is then an exploiter, and the sentence addresses debt and oppression.

debates.bearing: The difference is small in the argument of the chapter. In either reading the leaders mislead and the rulers exploit, and the people are being turned from their paths. The more important point is the plain statement that the LORD calls them 'My people,' as He does in verses 12, 14 and 15.

study.originalLanguages:
In verse 1 the LORD removes 'supply and support.' The two Hebrew words are masculine and feminine forms of the same noun, from the root meaning to lean on. The BSB footnote gives 'staff' for 'support.' So the verse names everything a society leans on and then lists both the leaning-posts of bread and water and the people who hold up the society. Isaiah uses the root again in Isaiah 10:20, where the survivors of Israel will 'no longer depend on him who struck them' but will 'truly rely on the LORD,' and in Isaiah 36:6 where Egypt is a splintered reed of a staff. The word thus belongs to a larger theme: what do you lean on? When the false staffs are removed, the only one left is the LORD.

Verse 7 has a quiet link back to chapter 1. The man refuses leadership with the words 'I am not a healer,' and the Hebrew term for healer is a binder, from a root meaning to bind up a wound, which the BSB footnote shows. In Isaiah 1:6 the wounds of the nation are 'neither cleansed nor bandaged,' and that bandaging is the same root. So the question of chapter 1, who will bind these wounds, receives its answer in chapter 3: no one wants the job. Ezekiel 34:4 repeats it as a charge against shepherds, 'You have not ... bound up the injured.' Isaiah 30:26 promises the day when the LORD Himself binds up the bruise of His people.

Verse 8 says Jerusalem 'has stumbled' and Judah 'has fallen,' two verbs of collapse that match the ruin of the leaders in the list. The same verse says they acted against 'His glorious presence.' The BSB footnote renders the Hebrew literally, 'defying the eyes of His glory,' which makes the offence personal. They defied the LORD to His face, in front of His eyes.

In verse 13 the LORD 'arises to contend' and 'stands to judge.' The language is of a court session opening: the LORD takes His place on His feet and the case begins, and the verb 'contend' belongs to the same legal vocabulary as the dispute of chapter 1. The legal term then gives way in verse 14 to the vineyard. The verb for 'devoured' is a word that can mean to burn or to graze and to eat down, as when livestock graze in a neighbour's field or vineyard, Exodus 22:5. In the vineyard song, Isaiah 5:1 to 7, the vineyard is the house of Israel. The leaders were supposed to tend it, and instead they stripped it bare like grazing herds. The verb will return in Isaiah 4:4 where God purifies Zion by 'a spirit of burning.'

Verse 15 says they 'grind the faces of the poor.' The word for 'grind' is the one used of milling grain on a handmill, Numbers 11:8, so the image is of faces pressed under a millstone. Notice that in verses 12, 14 and 15 God keeps saying 'My people.' It is He who owns those who are being ground.

For the daughters of Zion, the BSB footnote on verse 17 says the line may be read 'will uncover their secret parts.' Whatever the exact reading, the sense is humiliation by exposure. Isaiah 20:4 shows the same picture for captives led away with bared buttocks to their shame. And verse 24 has a footnote that the Hebrew text and the Dead Sea Scrolls differ at the end of the list of reversals. The Dead Sea reading is 'instead of beauty, shame,' and the traditional text has a word usually translated 'branding,' the mark put on slaves and captives. Both end in shame, the shame of the defeated.

Lastly, verse 18's word for finery is a form of the word for beauty or glory. In Isaiah 4:2 the same word returns for the 'glory' of Israel's survivors. What is stripped as pride is given back as a gift.

typology.type: The man who will not lead a ruined people, Isaiah 3:6-7
typology.fulfillment: A leaderless city looks for someone, anyone, with a cloak, and the man refuses because there is nothing in his house and he is no healer. The one who does come is the shepherd who is moved with compassion for people who are 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd,' Matthew 9:36. Where the man in Isaiah says 'Do not make me leader,' Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. The escalation is that He takes the leadership no one wants and pays for it with His life. The type falls short because the man of Isaiah is a reluctant, unqualified neighbour, while Christ is the willing, fully qualified Shepherd.

typology.type: The vineyard devoured and the poor ground down, Isaiah 3:14-15
typology.fulfillment: The elders were meant to tend the LORD's vineyard, and they stripped it. Jesus tells a parable in which the tenants of the vineyard seize and kill the servants and then the son, Mark 12:1 to 9, and He draws on the same vineyard story of Isaiah 5. The correspondence is of a trust betrayed by those who were given it. The escalation is that the Son Himself, not only the poor, is cast out and killed, and the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone, Mark 12:10. The type falls short in that the leaders of Isaiah's day were corrected by exile, while the final rejection leads to the cross and the opening of the kingdom to others.

typology.type: Beauty stripped and replaced with sackcloth, Isaiah 3:24
typology.fulfillment: The reversal of the finery pictures a fall from honour to shame. Christ undergoes the same exchange for the sake of others. Isaiah himself says of the Servant that 'He had no stately form or majesty,' Isaiah 53:2, and the soldiers stripped Jesus of His clothes at the cross and cast lots for them, John 19:23 and 24. He took our shame so that we would be clothed in His righteousness, 2 Corinthians 5:21 and Revelation 3:18. The type is not a prediction of Christ's clothing; it is a pattern of loss and exchange which He brings to completion. It falls short since Isaiah's women lose beauty for their pride, and Christ loses it for love.

typology.type: The seven women who plead for a name, Isaiah 4:1
typology.fulfillment: The women ask only to be called by a man's name, because their disgrace is the lack of one. In the larger story the church is a people with no name of her own, and she takes the name of Christ, Acts 4:12 and Ephesians 3:14 and 15. God tells the desolate city, 'Your husband is your Maker,' Isaiah 54:5, and Paul says that believers are betrothed to one husband, Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The escalation is that the one who offers His name does not need the women to provide for themselves, as they promised to do, because He provides the wedding garment, Revelation 19:7 and 8. The type falls short in that the desperate women of Isaiah only meet a human need, while the church is given a name that saves.

study.christ:
Isaiah 3 leads to Christ most plainly by the missing figure. The chapter is a catalogue of leaders removed and leaders who fail, and the effect on the reader is to ask who will lead. When Isaiah says that no one will want the burden, he is stating the problem that the rest of the book answers. A child will be born and the government will rest on His shoulders, Isaiah 9:6. A king will reign in righteousness, Isaiah 32:1. A shoot from the stump of Jesse will not judge by what He sees or hears, but with righteousness will judge the poor and decide with equity for the lowly, Isaiah 11:3 and 4. Each of those promises is a direct answer to a charge in chapter 3. Where the elders devoured the vineyard, He judges the poor with righteousness. Where the rulers misled the people, He is the way and the truth, John 14:6.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of shepherding. Ezekiel 34 takes up the charge of Isaiah 3 against the shepherds, and the LORD says there that He Himself will search for His sheep and bind up the injured, Ezekiel 34:11 and 16. Jesus presents Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life, John 10:11, and He sees the crowds as harassed and helpless sheep, Matthew 9:36. The thing the man in Isaiah 3:7 would not do, being a binder of wounds, is what Christ does. He heals the sick and binds up the broken, and in the end He bears wounds Himself: 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5.

It leads to Christ by the contrast of leadership. He teaches that rulers of the Gentiles lord it over people, but that among His followers whoever wants to be great must be a servant, and that the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom, Mark 10:42 to 45. The leaders of Isaiah 3 took from the poor and filled their houses. The Lord of the church gave Himself so that the poor might be rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9. And after His resurrection He tells Peter, who had failed, to feed His lambs and tend His sheep, John 21:15 to 17, which is the restoration of leadership in the way that Isaiah 3 declares impossible without a Saviour.

It leads to Christ in the stripping and the shame. The women lose their jewellery, and Christ is stripped at the cross. The shame of verse 24 is borne by the one who endured the cross and despised its shame, Hebrews 12:2. The Hebrew text of the verse speaks of branding, the mark of captives, and Paul says that Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13.

A caution applies. The passage does not mention the Messiah, and it would be wrong to find Him in the catalogue of ornaments or the details of the list. The links above come from the book's own promises in chapters 9, 11 and 32, from Ezekiel's treatment of the same charge, and from the New Testament's use of shepherd and servant language. What chapter 3 itself does is state the need so clearly that the reader cannot be satisfied with anyone less than the true Shepherd-King.
study.god:
Isaiah 3 begins with God as the supplier, which is not what a reader expects in an oracle of judgment. The things He removes are the things He had given: food and water, the soldier, the judge, the prophet and the elder. A society's stability is not a natural achievement; it is a gift, and the one who gives it can withdraw it. This tells us that God is the source of ordinary order and not only of miracles. It also means that to remove it, He needs only to stop holding it up.

He is the God who takes the side of the powerless. The courtroom scene of verses 13 to 15 is startling because of who is in the dock. He does not stand against the poor but against the elders and leaders who have grinded them down, and He does it with the phrase 'My people.' The ownership language is tender. Those being crushed belong to Him, and an injury to them is an injury to Him. This is the character of the God of the exodus, who heard the cry of the oppressed, Exodus 3:7 and Exodus 22:22 and 23, and it is the same God whom Mary sings about when He brings down rulers and lifts up the humble, Luke 1:52.

He is also a God of moral order, of sowing and reaping. Verses 10 and 11 say that the righteous will eat the fruit of their labour and the wicked will be repaid with what their hands have done. It is a principle by which the world is built, and Paul repeats it in Galatians 6:7. The judgment of the chapter is the working out of that order. It is not capricious, and it does not make the innocent fall with the guilty without distinction. The voice of verse 10 is almost tender: 'Tell the righteous it will be well with them.'

He is jealous of His glory. The sin of verse 8 is not only against people. It is 'defying His glorious presence,' defiance to His face. He takes the contempt of the proud personally because He is personally present. This ties the chapter to the earlier call in 2:11 and 17, that the LORD alone will be exalted.

He is a God who uses means. The removal of leaders comes through war and the political events that Isaiah's hearers would see unfolding. God's providence works in and through the human acts of invaders and rulers, without making Him the author of their sins. The same God who takes away is the God who will in 4:2 to 6 provide again.

For worship, this prompts a reflection on how we pray for those in authority. We pray for them, 1 Timothy 2:1 and 2, and we pray with an awareness of the standard they are held to. It also invites us to be honest about what we lean on. If God supplies and supports, then the proper response to a stable society is gratitude, and to a collapsing one, repentance and trust.

crossReferences.note: The rulers of chapter 1 love bribes and do not defend the fatherless, and the widow's plea never reaches them. Chapter 3 returns to the same people and gives the sentence. The two passages are one case, charged in chapter 1 and judged in chapter 3.

Woe to those who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left. It supplies the mechanism behind the plunder of the poor in 3:14, where the landowners absorb the holdings of others and live alone in the land. The accusation is economic, and the cause is greed.

The charge against those who enact unjust statutes and withhold justice from the oppressed of 'My people.' The same phrase appears in 3:12, 14 and 15, and here the legal machinery itself is turned against the weak, so that widows are prey and orphans plunder.

A younger contemporary asks rulers who should know justice why they tear the skin from the people and strip the flesh from their bones. The grinding of faces in Isaiah 3:15 finds a more graphic form in Micah's picture of the rulers as butchers.

The prophet to the exile takes up the shepherd image and accuses the shepherds of feeding themselves while the sheep go hungry. They did not strengthen the weak or bind up the injured, which is the very task Isaiah 3:7 says no one would take on.

The women of Samaria are called cows of Bashan who oppress the poor and ask their husbands for more to drink. It shows that the women of the ruling class could be a part of the culture of extraction, which explains why Isaiah addresses the daughters of Zion in the same oracle.

Complacent women are told to stand up and tremble, because the harvest will fail and the city will be abandoned. It is a second summons to the same group, and it shows that the warning of Isaiah 3:16 to 26 was not a single outburst but a repeated pastoral concern.

The elders of the Daughter of Zion sit on the ground in silence with dust on their heads and sackcloth on, and the young women bow their heads. It is the aftermath of the fall of Jerusalem, and it reads as the fulfilment of Isaiah 3:24 to 26 in the very postures the prophet predicted.

God is not mocked, and whatever a man sows he will reap. This restates the principle of Isaiah 3:10 and 11 for the church, and it shows that the moral order the prophet appeals to is not limited to Israel. It is how God governs people.

Jesus claims to be the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The claim stands against all the failed shepherds of Isaiah 3 and Ezekiel 34, and it fulfils the LORD's own promise to take over the care of His flock.

Peter charges elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for greed and not lording it over those entrusted to them. It is the corrected version of what Isaiah 3:14 and 15 condemns, and it shows how the New Testament carries the standard for leaders forward.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 3 belongs to the long story of leaders who fail the people they were given. It begins in Eden, where the first man was set to tend and keep the garden and failed to guard it, Genesis 2:15 and Genesis 3:6. It continues through the Judges, where 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' Judges 21:25, and through the kings of Israel and Judah, whose failures fill the books of Samuel and Kings. In that line Isaiah's elders and rulers are not unusual. They are a stage in a pattern that the Bible keeps returning to.

The chapter looks backward to the covenant. The Law set out a different kind of leadership: a king who did not multiply horses and silver, Deuteronomy 17:14 to 20, judges who did not take bribes, Deuteronomy 16:19, and a people who cared for the widow and the orphan, Deuteronomy 24:17 to 22. Isaiah 3 describes what happens when that law is ignored: a society in which the supports are knocked out and the poor are ground down. The curses of Deuteronomy 28 are the larger background, and the war and exile of verses 25 and 26 fit them.

It looks forward in two ways. It points to the exile, when the real removal came, 2 Kings 24:14, and to the return, when a remnant of the survivors came back. But the faithful leadership the prophets looked for did not arrive with the return. Nehemiah finds nobles exacting interest from their own people, Nehemiah 5:1 to 13. The second look forward is to Christ, who is both the answer to the leadership vacuum and its judge. He is the shepherd who gives His life, and the coming King of Isaiah 9 and 11 and 32.

For the church, the story continues in the shepherding of elders who are told not to lord it over the flock, and in the principle that to whom much is given, much will be asked. It also continues in the cry of the poor, whose wages and houses are seen by God, James 5:4.

In the new creation the situation is reversed. The Lamb on the throne is the shepherd of His people, 'and He will lead them to springs of living water,' Revelation 7:17. The city is not governed by the proud but by the one who was slain, and its people are no longer fatherless or widows. The women who wanted a name receive one: the people of God have His name written on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4. The jewels are not an ornament of pride but the foundation of the city, a gift that cannot be taken, Revelation 21:19.

quiz.q: What does God announce He will remove from Jerusalem and Judah in verses 1-3?

options.text: Every stabilizing leader and support, warriors, judges, elders, and counselors alike.
options.note: The list spans military, judicial, and social leadership, a comprehensive removal of societal structure.

options.text: Only the city's food supply.
options.note: Food and water are named, but the list quickly broadens to leadership roles as the main focus.

options.text: Only foreign mercenaries serving in the army.
options.note: The list names Judah's own native leaders, not foreign hires.

options.text: Only the religious prophets and diviners.
options.note: Prophets and soothsayers are included, but so are warriors, judges, elders, and counselors.

quiz.q: What does the reaction in verse 7, 'do not make me leader of the people,' reveal?

options.text: That the coming devastation will be so severe no one wants the burden of leading a ruined people.
options.note: This pictures total societal collapse, where leadership becomes a burden no one will accept.

options.text: That Judah had too many willing candidates for leadership.
options.note: The opposite is true; people refuse leadership because there is nothing left to lead.

options.text: That the man is being humble rather than desperate.
options.note: The context of ruin and lack of resources shows this is desperation, not modesty.

options.text: That foreign powers have already installed new rulers.
options.note: The scene pictures Judahites themselves scrambling, not a foreign installation of leadership.

quiz.q: What specific charge does the LORD bring against the elders and leaders in verses 14-15?

options.text: They devoured the vineyard entrusted to them and crushed the poor for personal gain.
options.note: The Hebrew riv, formal legal charge, names exploitation of the vulnerable directly.

options.text: They failed to build enough fortified cities.
options.note: The charge concerns injustice toward the poor, not military infrastructure.

options.text: They neglected the temple sacrifices.
options.note: The specific charge here is social and economic exploitation, not ritual neglect.

options.text: They were too lenient with criminals.
options.note: The charge is the opposite: they themselves oppressed and plundered the vulnerable.

quiz.q: What is the point of the long catalog of the daughters of Zion's finery in verses 18-23?

options.text: It pictures misplaced security and pride in luxury that will be entirely stripped away in judgment.
options.note: The detailed list heightens the shock of its total removal, echoing chapter 2's warning against trusting wealth.

options.text: It is simply a historical record of ancient jewelry styles.
options.note: The list serves a rhetorical, theological purpose within the judgment oracle, not mere antiquarian interest.

options.text: It proves that all personal adornment is sinful.
options.note: The point is misplaced trust and pride amid injustice, not that ornamentation itself is inherently wrong.

options.text: It shows God's approval of Judah's wealth and fashion.
options.note: The passage announces judgment on, not approval of, this display of luxury.

quiz.q: What does the closing image of 4:1, seven women grasping one man, communicate?

options.text: The devastating loss of men through war has left society desperate, willing to forgo normal expectations just to escape shame.
options.note: It closes the unit with the human cost of the judgment announced in 3:25, men falling by the sword.

options.text: A celebration of polygamous marriage as an ideal.
options.note: The scene depicts desperation and social collapse, not an endorsement of a marital ideal.

options.text: A promise of coming prosperity and abundance.
options.note: The women explicitly say they will provide their own food and clothing, a picture of scarcity, not abundance.

options.text: A metaphor unrelated to the surrounding judgment context.
options.note: It directly follows and depends on the preceding announcement that Judah's men would fall by the sword.

questions: God held Judah's leaders to a higher account for how they treated the poor. If you have any measure of authority or influence, how are you using it for those with less power than you?
The catalog of finery pictures a people preoccupied with appearance while their foundations crumbled. Where might you be polishing the surface of your life while ignoring deeper cracks?
No human leader in this chapter was willing to bear the people's burden. How does it change you to know Christ willingly bore that burden all the way to the cross for you?
The charge against the elders was vivid and personal: devouring the vineyard, grinding the faces of the poor. Where do you need to examine whether your comfort has come at someone else's cost?
Judah trusted in warriors, counselors, and luxury instead of the LORD, and all of it was stripped away. What supports are you leaning on that could be removed in a moment?

translationNotes.note: 'Supply and support' translates a Hebrew pair, mashen and mishenah, from the same root for a staff or support, a wordplay meaning something like every prop and every propping thing.

'Women rule over them' may describe literal weak or inexperienced leadership or function idiomatically for effeminate, incompetent rule; either way it signals a shameful reversal of expected order in that culture.

'Take away our disgrace' reflects the ancient Near Eastern shame of a woman remaining unmarried and childless; the women's request is a desperate bid for social legitimacy amid a catastrophic shortage of men.
